speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is my dream funeral wake which I regularly remind my husband to ensure that I will have if he is around to see it through.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yes, this is not a typical conversation between wives and husbands, less so for parents and children, maybe even be taboo, if brought up among some elders in our midst.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a recently launched book titled "Singapore Ageing: Issues and Challenges", co-edited by our former Member of Parliament, Dr Sushilan Vasoo.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The final chapter dealt aptly with end-of-life issues as its title – "Every Ending Requires Planning" – by co-authors Lee Geok Ling and Chee Wai Yee.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whilst the percentage who passed away at home improved to 39% in 2022, it is still some distance away from the desire of most Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Without destigmatising the conversations on end-of-life and normalising the understanding, decision-making and support for Singaporeans to die with the dignity of their choice, most of us would not be able to fulfil our final wish of the most definite event of our life.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With a fast-ageing population, this can increasingly be an issue.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will speak on two aspects of enhancing choices and dignity in end-of-life, namely, one, destigmatising the conversation and simplifying the planning; and two, increasing primary and community care options for supporting wishes of dying at home as far as one prefers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My fellow colleague on the Government Parliamentary Committee for Health, Mr Yip Hon Weng, will speak on caregiver support and the need for more possibility and flexibility in the subsidies for palliative care.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many Singaporeans may not appreciate the range of decisions that one needs to make regarding healthcare, legal and financial matters for one who is dying until a loved one confronts death.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Efforts have been made by the Government to introduce the Advanced Medical Directive (AMD) since 1997, the Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) through the Mental Capacity Act since 2008 and Advanced Care Planning (ACP) since 2011.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When I surveyed a group of about 40 active volunteers in my Jalan Kayu Constituency serving in the grassroots or at my Meet-the-People Session averaging at about 55 years old and above about a month ago in preparation for this speech, I found that the majority have not done any of these three instruments, with less than a handful with the LPA.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When I further inquired on their reasons, most said that they felt that there was no need at their age until much later or did not associate this as inter-related instruments for their self-determination on maintaining the preferred quality of life and dignity when we lose our mental or functioning abilities, especially in the end-of-life stage.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I explained to the group of active volunteers why I started annual health screening from the age of 40.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because I learned that risks of chronic diseases start from that age.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And why I signed my AMD and LPA in the last two years when I entered my 50s.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because of COVID-19 pandemic showed me the unforeseen fragility of health and life.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, most important of all, I shared that I only have one son and the last thing I want is to be a burden on him.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The volunteers understood and agreed to the need to sign these instruments for planning.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lucky for us, the lawyers among the group offered free certification to help the rest through the application process.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that MOH, MSF and AIC can provide integrated training resources to the network of over 100 Active Ageing Centres (AACs) around Singapore which will be increased to about 220 island-wide by 2025 to conduct such conversations periodically to help more Singaporeans talk about and simplify their planning on end-of-life choices.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, increasing primary and community care options for end-of-life support.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A small local study in 2012 with about 60 Singaporeans aged 50 years and above identified, I quote, "Having physical comforts at the end-of-life, avoiding an unnecessarily prolonged dying process, maintaining sensitivity towards religious and spiritual beliefs, avoiding burden on family, avoiding expensive care, being cared for by a trustworthy doctor, maintaining control over decisions and achieving a sense of completion." This brings me to the topic of palliative care.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The World Health Organization (WHO) defines palliative care as improving the quality of life of patients and that of their families who are facing challenges associated with life threatening illnesses.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: WHO further explains that palliative care involves a range of services developed by a range of professionals that all have equally important roles to play, including doctors, nurses, support workers, paramedics. pharmacists, physiotherapists and volunteers in support of the patient and their family.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: According to the Singapore Hospice Council, there are currently nine community organisations that provide home palliative care.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would elaborate on the first two issues while Mr Yip Hon Weng will cover the last two issues in his speech.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A study in 2018 showed that only half of the patients with advanced cancer were aware of palliative care support options.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A key indication or expression of preference for palliative home care is done through ACP, which I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, as I mentioned, the adoption level of ACP is currently still low.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, worldwide, only about 14% of people who need palliative care currently receive it.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The global need for palliative care will continue to grow because of the ageing of populations and the rising burden of noncommunicable and some communicable diseases.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are demographic trends and disease burden challenging Singapore as well.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Early delivery of palliative care can reduce unnecessary hospital admissions and the use of health services, thus managing healthcare costs increases.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to step up awareness and access to palliative care options in the coming years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, on the health, social and community players involved in palliative care support.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whether carried out in a hospital, hospice or home, the support today can involve several different teams and several different care providers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The identification of "being cared for by a trustworthy doctor" in the study on good end-of-life components which I mentioned earlier, is an important one to note.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, can family doctors be gradually enabled to become a central player in providing home palliative care for Singaporeans who prefer that.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The idea is in line with the spirit and principle of Healthier SG, the major multi-years initiative led by MOH to better manage the health of our ageing population and manage healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we succeed in facilitating for Singaporeans to enrol and build relationship with a trusted family doctor of their choice for long-term health management, surely this family doctor can be a most comforting main point of contact for medical advice relating to one's end-of-life care, if the family doctors are well-supported by home palliative care service providers, with integrated workflows from hospitals to homes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My wish, Mdm Deputy Speaker, for the near future, is for the Government to centrally support the piloting of such possibilities at every public and even private hospitals and hospices, and not just in one pro-active hospital like Ng Teng Fong General Hospital, integrating the workflows at some point with family doctors participating in Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So that, in the end, most Singaporeans can have the choice to end our walk on this world with dignity, peace and in the comfort of our home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This has allowed me to understand more about their lives, their aspirations as well as their challenges, so that I can better support their needs as their MP.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Understandably, the conversations at wakes are never easy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They revolve around the last days of their loved ones and for many, this includes the need for palliative care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many of the residents I have spoken to have confirmed that support for palliative care is still nascent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many just do not know what to do.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But as they say, you can fall ill many times, but you only die once.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We plan for so many other milestones in life, from marriage to birthdays and beyond.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But when it comes to our twilight years, many people refuse to face up to the inevitable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is also compounded by the belief that death is still considered a taboo subject in our Asian culture.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some well-meaning children may even worry that their parents or grandparents will think that they are cursing them, if they bring up the subject.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, we must overcome this reluctance and have an honest conversation about death and end-of-life care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is heartening to know that the clinical protocols in hospitals are being improved, and that healthcare providers are being upskilled to develop general palliative care capabilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am also pleased that there are also plans to engage in early conversations with patients and their loved ones on their wishes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, I will focus on what else we can do in terms of caregiver and financial support, and in making palliative care at home accessible, acceptable and affordable for all.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, caregivers are the bedrock of a community-based quality ageing experience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As Member Ms Ng Ling Ling has mentioned in her speech, many people prefer to die at home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Having plans such as ACP, LPA and AMD in place certainly help reduce the stress that may arise amongst family members and give clear directions for the caregiver.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, even with these plans in place, we still need to see how best to support the caregiver.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As mentioned earlier, many people are still not aware, or uncomfortable talking about end-of-life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This leads to a lot of dynamics amongst siblings, each wanting to do the best for their parents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the definition of "best", may not be aligned.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the end, there may not be a consensus.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Often, the ones who are left to provide for the care for those at end-of-life is the child who may not be married.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This can bring about a lot of negative emotions, such as resentment and overall helplessness, for being the one left to shoulder the burden alone.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, the support for the caregiver must also consider his or her emotional and mental health.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my Budget response speech this year, I highlighted that navigating the fragmented landscape of caregiver assistance and services can be overwhelming, especially for those who are limited in their English language proficiency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I suggested matching a dedicated care coordinator with a family.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These coordinators can guide caregivers to assess practical help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They can look out for their psychological well-being and provide timely interventions when needed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Through my interactions with my residents, I would like to highlight four areas to reduce the stress of caregiving.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Caregivers need to understand the illness of their loved ones, the trajectory of the illness, and what to expect as it progresses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They also need to know who to call for help, especially during a crisis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This knowledge can go a long way in reducing uncertainty, stress and anxiety for the caregiver.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Caregivers can learn a lot from each other.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It can be very helpful to understand and have emotional support from people who have gone through similar journeys.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Online support groups, even through simple means, such as organising through WhatsApp, is a great idea.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we need to figure out the logistics of setting it up and maintaining it, as well as ensuring that it is accessible to all who need it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, caregiver respite is important for those caring for loved ones that may require care for longer than a few months.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such services allow carers to take some time off, and to get emotional relief and help whilst ensuring that the patient is looked after.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some may even struggle to let go, despite family members offer to help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When their loved one passes on, some may even develop depression, if their support system is not there.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is why all palliative care service providers should provide or link caregivers to partners who can provide emotional support during and after the caregiving period.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is no secret that healthcare costs can be a huge burden on families, especially when dealing with end-of-life care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Extending the use of MediSave to patients receiving care at home is a good start.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: MOH has also set a goal to lower the percentage of people who pass away in hospitals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would require that hospitals and hospice councils offer affordable and accessible palliative care services to patients in their own homes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But I understand that there are plans to expand this to MOH-supported home medical and nursing providers who offer basic palliative care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry provide more information on this?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Another suggestion is to extend MedisSield Life to home hospice care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is also important to note that the cost of family caregiving is often not included in the healthcare financing model, even though families are often integral to care at the end of life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us not forget about the out-of-pocket expenses that can quickly add up.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is not just the cost of medications and supplies, but also transportation to and from hospital appointments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is there a concern that this may lead to undertreatment, or a denial of care that could compromise a patient's quality of life, particularly for patients with complex or chronic conditions, if providers feel that providing certain services will exceed the budget?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: After all, patients sometimes do outlive their prognosis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: In my response to the President's Address, I asked the House what does the "good life" look like.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Today, I would like to ask the opposite question – what is a "good death"?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Personally, unlike Ling Ling, I do not wish for fairy lights at my death bed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I believe I speak not just for myself, but for all my fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: End-of-life may be a sensitive topic to talk about, but it is an important one that will affect all of us.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The reality is that in Singapore, despite clear preferences for receiving end-of-life care and dying at home, only about one in four died at home over the past few years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: So, we do need to discuss issues surrounding palliative and hospice care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The hospice movement took root in Singapore in the 1980s.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Today, more than 20 institutions provide palliative care across various settings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our community providers supported some 8,800 individuals with life-limiting conditions in 2022.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is 30% more than in 2017, just five years ago.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have come a long way since the 1980s, but much more can be done.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Today, I will highlight three areas of work to enhance end-of-life care: first, improving access to palliative care; second, better supporting caregivers; and third, normalising conversations on death and dying.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With an ageing population, more will need palliative care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will invest in expanding our services and review our financing frameworks to improve access to palliative care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will train more doctors, nurses and allied health professionals in specialised palliative care, particularly in home care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are also setting aside palliative beds in upcoming community hospital developments to cater to the growing demand.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Beyond specialised services, we also want to entrench palliative care as a basic skill set for all healthcare professionals across disciplines and settings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will require us to change the mindsets and instincts of our clinicians and equip them with the necessary skills and tools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are working with the AIC and providers to do this, beginning with nursing homes and home care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We agree that in the longer term, family doctors can play a role, building on relationships forged with their enrolled patients.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are also working with hospitals and palliative care providers to implement workflows that Ms Ng Ling Ling spoke about, to enable more patients to undergo what we call a compassionate discharge back to home.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This involves, for instance, providing appropriate training and resources, and implementing hand-over checklists to ensure continuity of care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Yip asked about subsidies for professional palliative caregiving and extending MediShield Life to home hospice care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Patients can already tap on MediSave for in-patient, day hospice and home palliative care and make claims under MediShield Life for in-patient palliative care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Government-funded home medical and nursing providers whose patients are at the end-of-life stage, will soon be able to make MediSave claims for these patients, similar to home palliative care providers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition, palliative care providers have done well in raising significant charity dollars to complement Government funding and reduce out-of-pocket costs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are reviewing the overall financing framework for palliative care to ensure that affordability concerns do not deter anyone who needs palliative care from receiving it.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Yip also asked about shifting to a capitation funding model for palliative care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The scope of care included under capitation funding for the Regional Health Systems does not include community palliative care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Through a simpler funding formula, providers will be empowered to decide on the most appropriate care setting for the patient.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The pilot will also trial interventions to enable earlier referrals of patients with non-cancer conditions to community palliative care and care protocols, to better support them in community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If the outcomes are promising, we will consider how we can progressively mainstream it with appropriate safeguards to ensure continued quality of care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Caregivers are the most critical factor in enabling one to be cared for at home, but they often come under tremendous stress while coping with grief and loss.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have been continuously enhancing measures to support caregivers through this challenging journey.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We introduced the home-based respite care pilot, as part of the Caregivers Support Action Plan in 2019, to allow caregivers of end-of-life patients to rest or tend to other matters while their loved ones are cared for by palliative-trained care staff.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Since January 2023, hospitals can also refer patients to the service, so that patients and their caregivers can be supported more quickly upon discharge.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This takes a significant load off caregivers who often have to arrange for home modifications and adjust to new routines while dealing with the grief of soon having to say goodbye to a loved one.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Home-based respite care complements care provided by day hospices, which allow end-of-life patients with stable conditions to benefit from social activities and rehabilitation while allowing caregivers to take a break.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The four-day hospice centres today have adequate places to meet demand.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will monitor utilisation and expand capacity if required.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Indeed, end-of-life patients and their caregivers have unique needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Singapore Hospice Council (SHC) has developed and shared caregiver resources with hospitals and palliative care providers so that caregivers have the information on hand to better cope at home.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The SHC will also be setting up a helpdesk later this year, so that caregivers who need advice can call in to receive timely support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Apart from supporting caregivers with caregiving skills and knowledge, palliative care providers also support their emotional needs, linking them up with grief counsellors or support groups, if needed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is part of the care coordination role which palliative care providers play.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Other long-term care schemes, like CareShield Life, also provide cash payouts to eligible Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They may also withdraw up to $200 in cash every month from their own or their spouses' MediSave accounts under the MediSave Care scheme.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Terminally ill patients may also withdraw all their Central Provident Fund (CPF) savings in a lump sum under the CPF Reduced Life Expectancy scheme, subject to retaining a balance of $5,000 in their MediSave account.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On top of the schemes and services, we, ourselves, play an important role in ensuring that we have a good death.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We need to take charge of our own end-of-life journey, to be open to discussing with our loved ones what matters to us, what quality of life means and how we would want to live our last days.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will do more to normalise conversations about death and dying.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MOH and the Public Service Division (PSD) set up the My Legacy portal in 2020 to serve as a one-stop resource to provide information on planning ahead, and tools, such as the LPA, ACP and the AMD.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are looking at further digitalising these processes to make it more convenient for the public to make these tools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will be launched later this year and will involve a range of both in-person and digital activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To complement the campaign's activities, a series of workshops will be held at AACs, as Ms Ng Ling Ling has suggested.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are also working with SHC to engage the community through the grassroots, corporates, faith-based organisations and schools to build a pool of advocates.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Serving as a trusted source of information, these advocates can plant seeds of these important conversations amongst the wider community and spread awareness of palliative care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many decades ago, people routinely spent the last days at home.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They would deteriorate gradually and loved ones would gather as their activity levels drop.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Medical advancement has given us the belief that all conditions can be treated and life extended.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many end up dying in hospitals, having life-sustaining treatment up to their very last breath even though this might not have been how they wished to leave.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We now know that health is, to a large extent, determined by social factors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Death is, in fact, also very much a social process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: What matters to most is being with their loved ones in a familiar environment, having their final wishes fulfilled and regrets resolved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Bringing end-of-life conversations into our collective consciousness is similarly a social process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It builds on relationships and often evokes strong emotions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
